opus-5.5.text:
I think it's genuinely hard, and I'd be careful about declaring anyone has fully "escaped." What I've seen is companies that have bought themselves time and built something that's harder to replicate, which is a bit different.

The pattern that seems to work is when the application company owns something the model company doesn't naturally have. One is distribution and workflow: if you're deeply embedded in how a particular group of people work every day, like developers in their editor or lawyers with their documents, the switching cost isn't really about the model anymore. It's about habits, integrations, trust, data living in your system. The model is an ingredient, and you can swap ingredients.

The second is proprietary context or feedback. If your product generates a stream of signal about what "good" looks like in a narrow domain, signal that a general model company just doesn't see, you can turn that into an advantage, whether through fine-tuning, better evals, or better scaffolding around the model. That compounds in a way that a thin wrapper never does.

The companies that get squeezed are the ones whose value is basically "we prompted the model well" or "we stitched together a capability the model didn't have yet." Those gaps close every six months. Each new model release eats a layer of what used to be product.

So my honest view is that the safest position isn't trying to be smarter than the model. It's assuming the model will get much better and asking what you still own when that happens. If the answer is "nothing," you're not escaping, you're just early. If the answer is users, data, workflow, or a domain the big labs don't care enough about, then you have a real chance.

And one more thing: the model companies themselves have limited attention. They can't do everything. A lot of the space survives not because it's defensible in theory, but because it's not the top priority for any lab. That's a real moat in practice, even if it's not a comfortable one.

r001.rationale: The response discusses general strategies for application companies to resist being squeezed, but it does not identify Midjourney as an example.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the framing of "escaping" might be a little off. If you look at the companies that have done well as application layers—Cursor is the obvious example—they didn't escape model companies so much as they found a layer of value that the model companies either couldn't or didn't want to build themselves at the time. Cursor's early edge wasn't that they had a better model. They had a better understanding of what a developer actually wants to happen in the editor, the interaction design, the context management, the indexing of a codebase. Those are real engineering problems, and they're also problems where you accumulate data and user habits over time.

But I'd be careful about calling that a permanent escape. The model companies keep moving up the stack. Claude Code, Codex, these are the labs doing exactly what the application companies were doing a year earlier. So the question becomes: what does the application company own that a lab can't just replicate by releasing a product? I think there are roughly three things. One is distribution and user trust in a vertical that the labs don't care enough about to prioritize—legal, healthcare, specific enterprise workflows. Two is proprietary data or environment access, where the agent has to interact with systems that the lab doesn't have a relationship with. And three, which I think is underrated, is that the application company can be model-agnostic. If you're using three different models and routing between them, you have leverage that any single lab doesn't want you to have.

The companies I'd say have genuinely done something durable are the ones where the model is maybe thirty percent of the product and the other seventy percent is workflow, integration, and the feedback loop with real users. Perplexity is an interesting case—it's not clear to me whether they've escaped or whether they're just a few years ahead of being absorbed by search features inside the models. Midjourney actually escaped in a sense, because they trained their own model and built a community that the big labs didn't bother competing with on aesthetics.

So my honest answer is: a few have found temporary shelter, and the ones that will stay sheltered are the ones that keep redefining what the product is rather than being a thin wrapper that waits for the next model release. If your product gets better every time a new model comes out, and you didn't have to do anything, that's actually a warning sign. It means the model company could build you in a weekend.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says Midjourney “actually escaped in a sense,” but it does not identify Midjourney as a small application company.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by “escape.” If you mean building an application that model companies can’t easily replace, then the key question is: what do you own beyond access to the model?

If your product is essentially a prompt wrapped in an interface, a model update can erase a lot of your advantage. But if you own the user relationship, understand a particular workflow, and have a way to learn from whether the task actually succeeded, that’s a different position. Better models can make your product more useful without taking away the reason people use it.

I wouldn’t confidently name a company that has permanently escaped. The boundary is still moving. But I also don’t think using someone else’s model necessarily means being in their grasp. The real test is whether, when a better model comes out, users switch to that model directly—or your application gets better and they stay.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify Midjourney; it says it would not confidently name a company that has permanently escaped.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what you mean by “escape.” If an application’s value is mostly a thin layer around a model’s capabilities, then it’s vulnerable: the next model release can absorb what it does. But if it owns the workflow, the user relationship, and the feedback that comes from actually completing tasks, there’s room to build something durable.

I wouldn’t say there’s already a clear winner that has permanently escaped. The boundary keeps moving. A product might look defensible today, and then a stronger model makes much of its engineering unnecessary. The important question is whether better models make your product more valuable or make your product disappear.

So I don’t think application companies need to become independent of model companies. They need to own something beyond the model—especially a deep understanding of what users are trying to accomplish and a reliable way to accomplish it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses application companies generally but does not identify Midjourney as a possible example.
